OPS07-BP01 Perform post-incident analysis
A structured post-incident analysis examines the contributing
    factors behind a customer-impacting event and converts those
    findings into changes that reduce the chance of recurrence.
Desired outcome:
You run a consistent post-incident analysis for every
        customer-impacting event, triggered by your incident management
        process.
Your analysis identifies the multiple contributing factors
        behind an incident rather than a single root cause.
You capture the telemetry and timeline data needed to
        reconstruct what happened and when, and you automate its
        assembly so responders spend their time interpreting evidence
        rather than collecting it.
Your findings become tracked corrective actions with named
        owners and due dates, and a person remains accountable for each
        decision even when automation proposed it.
You share learnings across teams, so other workloads benefit
        from each incident.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams treat post-incident analysis as a search for who to blame,
        which discourages honest disclosure and hides the real
        contributing factors.
Responders resolve an incident and move on without recording the
        timeline, so the same failure recurs later with wider impact.
Organizations document a single root cause and stop, missing the
        chain of conditions that allowed the incident to happen.
Corrective actions are identified but never tracked to
        completion, so the analysis produces no lasting change.
Analysis happens only for the largest incidents, so smaller
        recurring incidents accumulate unaddressed.
Teams accept an automated root cause summary as the finished
        analysis, leaving the remaining contributing factors unexamined
        and the corrective actions unowned.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
You identify the components, conditions, and actions that
        contributed to an incident, which reveals concrete opportunities
        for improvement.
You reduce recurrence because corrective actions address
        contributing factors instead of symptoms.
You shorten future detection and recovery times by improving
        alarms, runbooks, and escalation paths based on evidence.
You build trust because a blameless approach encourages people
        to share what they observed.
You spread knowledge across teams, so improvements from one
        incident protect other workloads.
You complete analyses sooner, and for more incidents, because
        automation absorbs the evidence gathering while your team's
        effort goes to judgment and deciding what to change.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
High
Implementation guidance
A deployment, a latent configuration error, a missing alarm, and a
      slow escalation can combine into an event that no single fix could
      avoid. Look for the
contributing factors
—
      the set of conditions and actions that together allowed the
      incident.
When people expect blame, they withhold detail, and the analysis
      lacks the information it needs. A
blameless
approach assumes responders acted reasonably on what they knew at
      the time and focuses on the system and process gaps that allowed
      the incident. Amazon uses a structured Correction of Error (COE)
      process built on this principle.
Reconstruct the timeline and record key measurements. Detection
      time is the gap between when the incident began and when an alarm
      or person noticed. Time to engage is how long it took to get the
      right responders involved. Time to mitigate and time to resolve
      measure how long customers felt the impact. These intervals let
      you ask whether detection was slow or the response was slow once
      detected. Your observability and logging must capture the
      underlying timestamps.
Timeline point
What it marks
Incident start
When customer impact actually began
Detection
When an alarm or person first noticed the impact
Engagement
When the right responders were involved
Mitigation
When customer impact was halted or reduced
Resolution
When the incident was fully resolved
Decide who facilitates the analysis, on what cadence you review
      findings, and which incidents warrant a full analysis. Analyzing
      every minor incident is expensive and dilutes attention. Ignoring
      small recurring incidents is dangerous, because a pattern of small
      failures often precedes a large one. By default, analyze every
      customer-impacting incident and any near miss that could have been
      severe. Tailor what you share to the audience: give engineering
      teams the technical detail, and give business stakeholders the
      impact and remediation.
Split the work: automation collects evidence, people apply
      judgment. Assembling the timeline, correlating deployments and
      configuration changes with the incident window, and pulling logs
      and metrics is mechanical, time-consuming work suited to
      automation. Judgment and accountability stay with named people.
      They decide which conditions contributed, judge what is worth
      changing, weigh a fix's cost against the risk it removes, and
      commit to own that fix.
Treat an agent's probable-cause summary as a starting hypothesis
      backed by evidence. Keep a human review step that asks what else
      had to be true for this incident to happen, and record the
      corrective actions under the names of the people who will complete
      them.
Use your team's existing incident tracking system. Trigger the
      analysis consistently, reconstruct the timeline from evidence, and
      track corrective actions to completion in that system.
AWS Systems Manager OpsCenter
can hold corrective actions as
      OpsItems alongside your other operational work. Many teams use a
      third-party incident management or ticketing system instead.
Use the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) approach to feed
      incident findings back into your readiness criteria.
Creating ORR guidance from an incident
walks through turning a
      single incident into a reusable readiness question. AWS
couples its COE process to its ORR checklists
so each incident
      produces new readiness checks.
Implementation steps
Trigger the analysis from your
            incident process:
Make post-incident analysis a
            defined step in incident management, so it starts once a
            customer-impacting incident is closed rather than depending
            on manual follow-up. Confirm the scope criteria that decide
            which incidents and near misses receive a full analysis, and
            name who facilitates.
Reconstruct the timeline with
            metrics:
Collect the deployment changes,
            configuration changes, incident start time, alarm time,
            engagement time, mitigation start time, and resolution time.
            Correlating deployment and infrastructure change events with
            the incident window cuts the manual effort of evaluating
            potential causes.
AWS DevOps Agent
can do much of this correlation for you,
investigating an incident
across metrics, logs, and API change
            history and maintaining an investigation timeline you can
            carry into the analysis. Place these points on a single
            timeline so that detection, engagement, mitigation, and
            resolution intervals are visible and comparable.
Identify contributing factors
            without blame:
Work through the timeline to find
            the conditions and actions that combined to produce the
            incident. Assume responders acted reasonably on the
            information available, and document system and process gaps
            rather than individual fault. Amazon's
Correction of Error (COE)
process is a working example of this
            blameless approach. Bring in all parties connected to the
            incident, including the people who support the system,
            customer advocates, and those affected internally, and
anonymize the findings
so the record cannot be read as
            assigning blame.
Where an agent has already investigated, open the discussion
            with its output rather than a blank page. DevOps Agent
            publishes a root cause summary with the observations
            supporting it and the investigation gaps it encountered.
            Read the gaps as carefully as the conclusion, and have the
            group work outward from that hypothesis to the other
            conditions that had to hold for the incident to occur.
Ask targeted improvement
            questions:
Once the timeline is settled, work
            through four areas of questioning, following the structure
            Amazon uses in its
COE process
. For
detection
, ask when
            and how you learned there was customer impact, and what
            would halve the time to detect. For
diagnosis
, ask what underlying
            condition caused the impact and what would halve the time to
            diagnose. For
mitigation
, ask how you
            determined where to intervene, how you knew service was
            restored, and what would halve the time to mitigate. For
prevention
, ask not just what happened
            but why the underlying causes were possible.
Drive prevention questions past the
            first answer:
Apply the
5 Whys
to each candidate cause, asking why at each
            level until you have the full chain of conditions rather
            than the first plausible explanation. Keep it blame-free by
            pursuing why rather than who. Where an answer is
            "human error," treat that as a signal to ask
            why the error was possible, since it usually indicates a
            missing validation or fail-safe. Continue past five whys if
            the chain demands it, and plan a remediation for each
            answer, not only the last one.
Create and track corrective
            actions:
Convert each finding into a specific
            action stating its priority, the person responsible, and a
            due date, and track it to completion in your normal
            work-tracking system so it competes for priority alongside
            other work. Amazon's COEs average six to eight action items
            against an internal SLA measured in weeks, which is a useful
            sanity check on whether your analysis produced a realistic
            amount of work. Treat unfinished actions as open risk,
            because an analysis that produces no completed change
            delivers no value.
Communicate findings to the right
            audiences:
Publish the analysis where teams can
            find it, and tailor the message to each audience. Give
            engineering teams the technical detail and contributing
            factors, and give business stakeholders the customer impact
            and the remediation plan. The
resilience lifecycle "Respond and learn" stage
describes sharing these reports widely across the business
            so other teams benefit.
